title: How To Reignite Your Love Of Teaching
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin responds to what he describes as a culture of increasing pressure and stress across the teaching profession with a three-part framework for reclaiming enjoyment of the job. He advises focusing exclusively on what can be controlled and quickly accepting mandates or policies outside one's control rather than ruminating on them; recognizing that far more is actually within a teacher's control than commonly assumed, including classroom conditions often blamed on external factors; and centering the relational and instructional core of teaching — the actual act of enjoying students — as the thing that makes everything else fade into the background. He acknowledges that teaching has become genuinely harder in recent years but insists that with the right attitude and management approach, it remains rewarding. The piece closes with a call to 'love your job anyway' despite systemic frustrations shared by colleagues.
points: A three-part framework for reigniting enthusiasm: focus only on what's controllable, recognize that more is controllable than commonly assumed, and center the relational core of teaching.
Getting worked up over uncontrollable mandates (new programs, class-size policies) is self-sabotage that heightens their emotional importance unnecessarily.
Teachers who struggle most with stress tend to underestimate how much of their daily experience — student motivation, work habits, classroom tone — is actually within their control.
Focusing on genuinely enjoying relationships with students shrinks the perceived importance of external frustrations and policy complaints.
Even amid a broader culture of increased pressure in teaching, the right attitude and management approach can preserve real enjoyment of the job.
quotes: It’s official. A culture of pressure and stress has infected the teaching profession. It’s palpable in school after school and district after district.

Much of the stress teachers experience is due to things beyond their control. If it’s something you must do, like a mandate from administration, then it’s self-sabotage to get worked up about it—or even give it a second thought.
Teachers who struggle the most with stress and dissatisfaction assume that very little is within their control.
When you focus on enjoying your students, when you savor the relationships, the connections, and the act of teaching them, all that other stuff you're preoccupied with will fade away.

I hear from frustrated teachers every day who believe that they’re boxed in and have no options. But in every case, they’re upset over things that are either completely under their control or needn’t have any affect on enjoying their job.

It may not be as easy being a teacher as it once was, even five years ago. But with the right attitude and classroom management approach, and a healthy dose of shrewdness, it can be every bit as fun and rewarding.
